arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Butler argued the Minnesota Supreme Court incorrectly claimed federal law prevented it from deciding prisoner access.
Mr. Diamond asserted federal law controls the retroactivity of new constitutional rulings.
Justice Roberts noted Teague exceptions depend on the nature of the underlying right.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests whether federal law dictates when new constitutional rules apply to old convictions. the side that brought the case seeks uniform national standards. the opposing side defends state autonomy in applying these rules.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to mandate federal retroactivity rules for all states.
the opposing side wants the Court to allow states to set their own retroactivity standards.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues federal law exclusively controls the retroactivity of new constitutional rulings.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This dispute defines the balance between federal uniformity and state judicial power. It determines whether prisoners nationwide receive identical access to new constitutional protections. The outcome shapes the finality of criminal convictions across the country.
